new.title: Walk the gardens of Vaux-le-Vicomte, where Versailles began
new.desc: Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's finance minister, built this château between 1658 and 1661 with Le Vau, Le Brun and Le Nôtre. After his lavish party on 17 August 1661 the king had him arrested, then hired the same three men to create Versailles. Le Nôtre's gardens stretch for about 3 km and use forced perspective to look closer than they are.
new.tip: Climb the grand staircase of the house for the best view down the garden. Allow half a day and check the seasonal opening days before you go.
new.q: Château de Vaux-le-Vicomte, Maincy

new.title: Climb the keep of the Château de Blandy-les-Tours
new.desc: A medieval fortress begun in the 13th century and strengthened in the 14th under royal orders, with a gatehouse, drawbridge and three great round towers. Visitors can climb the donjon and walk the wall-walk. In 1707 Marshal de Villars turned it into a farm and had the tower roofs removed.
new.tip: Climb to the wall-walk for the view over the Brie plain. Sunday afternoons in the warmer months often bring theatre, music or circus in the courtyard.
new.q: Château de Blandy-les-Tours, Blandy

new.title: Tour the château de Champs-sur-Marne, a Pompadour pleasure house
new.desc: Built between 1699 and 1707 by Pierre Bullet and his son for Louis XIV's financiers, this is a textbook French maison de plaisance with a rotunda facing the garden. Madame de Pompadour rented it from 1757 to 1759, and from 1959 to 1971 General de Gaulle received visiting heads of state here. It has served as a filming location for about 80 productions.
new.tip: Combine it with the park walk. The château is run by the national monuments service, so check hours and closing days first.
new.q: Château de Champs-sur-Marne, Champs-sur-Marne

new.title: Spot the Rothschild palace of Ferrières from its grounds
new.desc: Baron James de Rothschild had Joseph Paxton build this Neo-Renaissance château from 1855 to 1859, reportedly telling him to build a Mentmore but twice the size. Its central hall is about 37 m long and 18 m high under a glass skylight. Bismarck negotiated here with Jules Favre in 1870, and Salvador Dalí attended a famous Surrealist Ball in 1972.
new.tip: Today it houses a hospitality school with two restaurants, so check the school's website for booking and visiting arrangements before you go.
new.q: Château de Ferrières, Ferrières-en-Brie

new.title: Find the real Guermantes behind Proust's famous name
new.desc: The château of Guermantes has been a listed monument since 1944. It inspired the name Marcel Proust gave to the duchess and the family in In Search of Lost Time, although the château itself never appears in the novel.
new.tip: It is a quiet place for literary fans and is close to Ferrières. Check whether visits are open on the day you plan to come.
new.q: Château de Guermantes, Guermantes

new.title: Look up at the Saint-Étienne cathedral of Meaux
new.desc: Begun around 1175 and finished in 1540, the cathedral has a 60 m north tower, a Flamboyant rose window and a warm stone from Varreddes. Bishop Bossuet, the Eagle of Meaux, lies beneath a black marble slab in the choir. The organ case dates from 1627.
new.tip: Walk into the choir to find Bossuet's tomb, then step out to the bishops' garden. Free to enter.
new.q: Cathédrale Saint-Étienne, Place Charles de Gaulle, Meaux

new.title: Stroll the bishops' garden behind Meaux cathedral
new.desc: The episcopal palace stands across a large courtyard from the cathedral, and Bossuet lived here when he was bishop of Meaux from 1682 to 1704. The palace has private gardens that give a calm green corner in the old cathedral quarter.
new.tip: Pair it with the cathedral and the cheese museum on the same square. Check garden opening hours first.
new.q: Jardin Bossuet, Meaux

new.title: Walk a 100 m trench at the Musée de la Grande Guerre
new.desc: About 75,000 objects and documents, mostly from the Jean-Pierre Verney collection, tell the story of the First World War from every side. The building cantilevers from the foot of the 26 m American Memorial of Meaux, and a 100 m trench with a no man's land has been recreated inside. The Battle of the Marne was fought right around Meaux in 1914.
new.tip: Allow two to three hours and finish on the rooftop terrace. A good rainy day choice.
new.q: Musée de la Grande Guerre du pays de Meaux, Meaux

new.title: Sleep in spirit at the Auberge Ganne in Barbizon
new.desc: In 1834 the Ganne family turned a farm into a grocery, then an inn, and the painters of the Barbizon school lodged here. The ground floor recreates their world with painted furniture, and upstairs dormitories have walls covered in sketches. The museum holds about a hundred works by Rousseau, Millet, Díaz, Troyon and Rosa Bonheur.
new.tip: Visit the neighbouring Théodore Rousseau house for temporary shows. Check opening days, as museums here close one day a week.
new.q: Musée des Peintres de Barbizon, 92 Grande Rue, Barbizon

new.title: Step into the Gothic church of Notre-Dame in Moret
new.desc: Built between the 12th and 15th centuries, the church of Moret has a Renaissance organ case that is a listed monument. It stands in a walled town where Alfred Sisley painted the Loing, the old bridge and the church itself.
new.tip: Take it on a walk down Rue Grande from the Porte de Samois. Free to enter when open.
new.q: Église Notre-Dame, Moret-sur-Loing

new.title: Pass through the Porte de Bourgogne in Moret
new.desc: Moret-sur-Loing keeps parts of its 12th and 15th century walls and two gates. The Porte de Bourgogne guards the approach from the Loing, while the Porte de Samois, also called the Porte de Paris, is a 15th century gate facing Fontainebleau.
new.tip: Walk from one gate to the other along Rue Grande for the whole old town in twenty minutes.
new.q: Porte de Bourgogne, Rue Grande, Moret-sur-Loing

new.title: Look up at the 12th century keep of Moret
new.desc: The donjon of the former château of Moret dates from the 12th century. It was partly destroyed during the Revolution and remodelled in the 19th century. It stands in the old town near the Loing bridge, where tradition credits Julius Caesar with an earlier crossing, though that is not established.
new.tip: Combine with a walk across the old bridge for the classic view of the town on the water.
new.q: Donjon, Rue du Donjon, Moret-sur-Loing

new.title: Visit Alfred Sisley's tomb under a forest sandstone rock
new.desc: Sisley settled in Moret in February 1889 and died there on 29 January 1899. He is buried beside his wife under a sandstone rock from the Fontainebleau forest, with a line from his own words about objects being wrapped in light. A monument to him was inaugurated in the town in 1911.
new.tip: Be respectful in the cemetery. Follow it with a visit to the Sisley bust beside the Porte de Samois.
new.q: Cimetière de Moret-sur-Loing, Moret-Loing-et-Orvanne

new.title: Explore the old château of Nemours and its museum
new.desc: A museum opened in 1903 inside the old château, saved from demolition by a sculptor, a painter and an engraver. It now holds more than 25,000 objects, from fine art and photography to manuscripts and minerals, and has a Musée de France label. A permanent route shows a bourgeois salon and a sculptor's studio.
new.tip: Check temporary exhibition dates and closing days. Afterwards cross to the riverside for a drink with a castle view.
new.q: Château-Musée de Nemours, Nemours

new.title: Visit the Saint-Mathurin basilica in Larchant
new.desc: Saint Mathurin's tomb drew a major medieval pilgrimage, and kings including Charles IV in 1325 and Henri IV in 1599 came here. A ceremony still takes place at the basilica on Whit Monday. The village belonged to the chapter of Notre-Dame de Paris until the Revolution.
new.tip: The village sits on the southern edge of the forest and is close to the Dame Jouanne rock. Free to look around.
new.q: Basilique Saint-Mathurin, Larchant

new.title: Count the screaming heads in Champeaux collegiate church
new.desc: One of the largest Gothic churches in the Paris region, 65 m long and begun around 1160. Carved screaming heads decorate the corbels of the choir, a green man sits near the transept, and one keystone shows a monkey lying in a basket. The Renaissance choir stalls are notable.
new.tip: Bring binoculars or a camera zoom for the carvings. Free to enter when open.
new.q: Collégiale Saint-Martin, Rue du Cloître, Champeaux

new.title: Find Templar paintings at the Commanderie of Coulommiers
new.desc: Founded between 1172 and 1173, this is one of the best preserved commanderies in France and the most complete north of the Loire. The Gothic chapel has paintings from about 1210 including Saint George slaying the dragon, and the dovecote holds 393 nesting boxes. A medieval garden has about 250 plants known in the Middle Ages.
new.tip: Opening is run by volunteers, so check the schedule. The main house is closed for restoration.
new.q: Commanderie des Templiers, Coulommiers

new.title: Descend into the Merovingian crypts of Jouarre abbey
new.desc: Founded in the 7th century around 630 to 635, the abbey keeps some of the best preserved Merovingian remains in France. The Saint-Paul crypt has carved capitals and the tombs of Saint Telchide, Saint Agilbert and the Irish princess Osanne. The abbey has been a listed monument since 1840.
new.tip: Check visiting hours for the crypts, as access is limited. A Benedictine community still lives here.
new.q: Abbaye Notre-Dame, Jouarre

new.title: Visit the Menier chocolate mill at Noisiel
new.desc: The Moulin Saulnier by the Marne was rebuilt by Jules Saulnier in the early 1870s with a load-bearing metal facade. The Menier family had run the site since 1825, and a workers' estate was built from 1874 to 1911. The reinforced concrete Cathedral building on the river was added around 1906 to 1908.
new.tip: Join the guided visit of the mill, which lasts about 90 minutes and does not include tasting. Check booking details with the tourist office.
new.q: Moulin Saulnier, Chemin de la Rivière, Noisiel

new.title: Cross the little bridges of Crécy-la-Chapelle
new.desc: Nicknamed the Venice of the Brie because the Grand Morin splits into many small arms between lanes and under bridges. Lavoirs, old mills and a belfry sit along the water. The Gothic collegiate church of Notre-Dame de l'Assomption, begun in the 13th century, has been a listed monument since 1846.
new.tip: Walk the riverside path from the belfry past the footbridges. Spring to early autumn is best.
new.q: Collégiale Notre-Dame de l'Assomption, Crécy-la-Chapelle

new.title: Stand on the medieval bridge at Grez-sur-Loing
new.desc: The old bridge over the Loing was built between the 12th and 14th centuries and was restored in 1980. Scandinavian, British, American and Japanese painters came to Grez from the 1860s. Next to it the Tour de Ganne, built by Louis VI in 1127, still stands.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk to the tower. A classic spot for sketching or photos in the morning light.
new.q: Vieux Pont, Grez-sur-Loing

new.title: Imagine the artists' colony at the Hôtel Chevillon in Grez
new.desc: After Corot, artists from Scandinavia, Britain, the United States and Japan stayed at the Hôtel Chevillon and the Pension Laurent to paint outdoors. The composer Frederick Delius and the painter Jelka Rosen lived in Grez from 1902, Carl Larsson met his wife here, and Robert Louis Stevenson met his future wife Fanny.
new.tip: Walk from the old bridge along Rue Wilson. The village is small, so it fits a short stop.
new.q: Hôtel Chevillon, Rue Wilson, Grez-sur-Loing

new.title: Find the ruined Franchard hermitage and the Eye of Nations
new.desc: A first hermitage was built here in the 12th century and largely destroyed during the Hundred Years War. It was rebuilt in 1676 and abandoned in 1717 by royal order, and a forest guard house stands on the ruins. Nearby the Eye of Nations, an oak heart ringed in bronze, marks the founding of the IUCN at Fontainebleau in 1948.
new.tip: Park at the Gorges de Franchard car park on the D301. Part of the forest burned in July and some sectors were closed, so check the ONF map of closed zones before you set out.
new.q: Croix de Franchard, Route de l'Ermitage, Fontainebleau

new.title: Visit Notre-Dame collegiate church on Melun's island
new.desc: The Île Saint-Étienne is the historic heart of Melun and holds the collegiate church of Notre-Dame, founded in the 11th century, together with the 11th century priory of Saint-Sauveur and traces of the old fortifications. Melun's own museum sits in the old Hôtel de la Vicomté, once Nicolas Fouquet's house.
new.tip: Cross the river and continue to the Saint-Aspais church for a Flamboyant Gothic contrast.
new.q: Collégiale Notre-Dame, Rue de la Courtille, Melun

new.title: Walk past the château of Bourron and the painters' church
new.desc: The château of Bourron followed a late 16th century project and was completed about twenty years later. Bourron-Marlotte drew painters from Corot onward, and the 12th century Saint-Sévère church has been listed since 1926. Renoir painted the tavern of Mère Antony here in 1866.
new.tip: Look at the exterior from the avenue and then walk into Marlotte village. Check whether the château grounds are open.
new.q: Château de Bourron, Avenue Blaise de Montesquiou, Bourron-Marlotte

new.title: Admire the cast iron Halle aux Fromages of Coulommiers
new.desc: Built in 1887 as the place where Brie cheeses were traded and sold, this cast iron hall was designed by Jules Chevallier on the model of the Paris Halles. It was labelled regional heritage in 2019. Coulommiers cheese trading is recorded from the 15th century.
new.tip: A good place to start a cheese day. Check the hall's event dates, as it hosts a cheese festival.
new.q: Halle aux Fromages, Cours Gambetta, Coulommiers

new.title: Spend a day at Disneyland Park
new.desc: Disneyland Park opened on 12 April 1992, with Sleeping Beauty Castle as its icon. Space Mountain opened in 1995 and Big Thunder Mountain Railroad runs about 1,500 m at 65 km/h. The resort is Europe's most visited theme park.
new.tip: Book tickets online and arrive before opening. Val d'Europe and Marne-la-Vallée stations on the RER A are right by the gate.
new.q: Disneyland Park, Chessy

new.title: Ride the film worlds of Disney Adventure World
new.desc: Originally opened on 16 March 2002 as Walt Disney Studios Park with rides themed to film and show business. It was renamed Disney Adventure World when the World of Frozen land opened, with Arendelle, the Frozen Ever After boat ride and a 36 m mountain.
new.tip: Go early for the biggest rides. A two park ticket lets you hop between both parks.
new.q: Disney Adventure World, Chessy

new.title: Stroll Disney Village after dark
new.desc: Disney Village is the resort's entertainment district of restaurants, shows and shops, and is part of the wider Disneyland Paris resort. You can visit without a park ticket.
new.tip: It stays lively into the evening, so come for dinner after the parks close.
new.q: Disney Village, Chessy

new.title: Hunt for bargains at La Vallée Village outlet
new.desc: A designer outlet in Serris, next to Disneyland Paris, with around a hundred fashion and lifestyle brands. It is open every day of the year except 25 December and 1 May, usually from 10 am to 8 pm.
new.tip: Take the RER A to Val d'Europe, one stop before Disneyland. Weekdays are quieter.
new.q: La Vallée Village, Cours de la Garonne, Serris

new.title: Meet snow leopards and tigers at Lumigny Safari Reserve
new.desc: A 92 hectare zoo with over 600 animals of about 90 species, billing itself as the largest diversity of big cats on one site in the world. Walk five circuits or take the Trans'félins train, see a 3 hectare cheetah enclosure with a 360 degree platform, and watch lemurs on two islands.
new.tip: Wear walking shoes and allow a full day. Check seasonal opening days before you go.
new.q: Lumigny Safari Reserve, Lumigny-Nesles-Ormeaux

new.title: Swim and paddle at the Jablines-Annet leisure island
new.desc: A regional leisure island of about 450 to 500 hectares with a lake of around 175 hectares of water and a white sand beach. Activities include kayaks, pedal boats, paddle boards, a cable ski and a treetop park.
new.tip: Swimming is supervised only in summer, so check dates. Reachable by train and bus without a car.
new.q: Île de loisirs de Jablines-Annet, Jablines

new.title: Watch rowers at the Olympic nautical stadium of Vaires-sur-Marne
new.desc: The Île-de-France nautical stadium hosted the canoe, kayak and rowing events of the Paris Games and includes whitewater courses of 300 m and 150 m. It was inaugurated in 2019 and belongs to the Vaires-Torcy leisure island, which offers activities to the public.
new.tip: Check the leisure island's programme for public sessions. Reach it by RER A or Transilien P.
new.q: Stade nautique olympique, Vaires-sur-Marne

new.title: Paddle the Loing beneath Moret's old bridge
new.desc: The Loing meets the Seine here, and the Moret tourist office lists canoeing and kayaking among its outdoor sports, with three routes on the river including a two hour outing. The old town rises above the water behind the bridge and the old mill.
new.tip: Ask the tourist office at the Porte de Samois for current operators and prices, as these change.
new.q: Pont de Moret-sur-Loing, Moret-sur-Loing

new.title: Walk the painters' trail through the oaks of Bas-Bréau
new.desc: A short loop of about 2 km from the Bas-Bréau car park passes the Lantara dormoir in the tall oaks, the Rocher Corot, the Chêne Sully, a medallion to Millet and Rousseau and a rock shaped like an elephant. It follows the paths of the Barbizon school painters.
new.tip: Wear shoes with grip. Part of the forest burned in July and some sectors were closed, so check the ONF map of closed zones before you set out.
new.q: Carrefour du Bas-Bréau, Route François Millet, Fontainebleau

new.title: Hike the sandstone Gorges d'Apremont
new.desc: The gorges are a landscape of rocks and platforms a few kilometres from Fontainebleau and a bouldering area with several hundred boulders. A loop of about two and a half hours starts from the Bas-Bréau crossroads and passes the Caverne des Brigands.
new.tip: The Auberge de la Caverne at the Bas-Bréau crossroads offers drinks. Part of the forest burned in July and some sectors were closed, so check the ONF map of closed zones before you set out.
new.q: Gorges d'Apremont, Fontainebleau

new.title: Follow the George Sand oak trail in the Gorges de Franchard
new.desc: The trail runs from the George Sand oak to the Eye of Nations and takes in moors, high oak woods and boulders. George Sand came here in 1833 with Alfred de Musset. The medium difficulty trail is free and open all year.
new.tip: Start from the Gorges de Franchard car park on the D301. Part of the forest burned in July and some sectors were closed, so check the ONF map of closed zones before you set out.
new.q: Parking des Gorges de Franchard, Fontainebleau

new.title: Walk the 5.5 km marked trail in the park of Champs
new.desc: The 85 hectare park mixes French and English garden styles and carries the Jardin remarquable label. A marked walk of about 5.5 km runs through it, past gardens recreated by the Duchêne brothers in 1895.
new.tip: Allow two hours. Check the park's opening hours, which can differ from the château.
new.q: Parc du château de Champs-sur-Marne, Champs-sur-Marne

new.title: Follow Sisley's footsteps on a guided walk in Moret
new.desc: The Moret Seine and Loing tourist office runs a Sur les pas de Sisley tour of the places where the Impressionist painted, as well as a historic walk of the town. It starts beside the Sisley bust near the Porte de Samois.
new.tip: Book through the tourist office at 4 bis place de Samois, as tour dates change by season.
new.q: Office de Tourisme Moret Seine et Loing, 4 bis place de Samois, Moret-sur-Loing

new.title: Stand at the foot of the Dame Jouanne rock
new.desc: The Dame Jouanne is described as the highest and most famous climbing rock in the Fontainebleau massif. It stands near the village of Larchant on the southern edge of the forest.
new.tip: Combine it with the Saint-Mathurin basilica in Larchant. Part of the forest burned in July and some sectors were closed, so check the ONF map of closed zones before you set out.
new.q: Dame Jouanne, Larchant

new.title: Walk the Loing and Seine loop from Saint-Mammès
new.desc: A walk of about 10 km starts from the river port of Saint-Mammès, follows the Loing to the medieval town of Moret and returns along the Seine. The Moret area has about 200 km of marked trails with information panels.
new.tip: The tourist office provides maps. Spring and summer are best, when the banks come alive.
new.q: Port de Saint-Mammès, Saint-Mammès

new.title: Cycle the Brie from Coulommiers to Crécy-la-Chapelle
new.desc: A stage of the three day Brie by bike route links Coulommiers with the canals of Crécy-la-Chapelle. It is about 28 km with around 265 m of climbing, mostly on small roads, in moderate difficulty.
new.tip: Download the GPX from the Seine-et-Marne tourism site. Start at Coulommiers station.
new.q: Gare de Coulommiers, Coulommiers

new.title: Taste Brie de Meaux at its own museum
new.desc: The Maison du Brie de Meaux follows the cheese from milk collection to the maturing cellar and explains its protected origin. The Brie de Meaux has a confrérie of brothers who wear robes that echo the cheese's round shape. Tastings are offered on weekends only.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Sunday with a lunch break. The shop is open without a ticket.
new.q: Maison du Brie de Meaux, 5 place Charles de Gaulle, Meaux

new.title: Watch Brie being made at the Fromagerie Saint-Faron
new.desc: The dairy's flagship Brie de Meaux Terre de Meaux is made from the raw milk of 12 local producers, moulded by hand and matured for at least 7 weeks. The tour includes a film, the cheesemaking floor, a tasting and the shop. It also makes Brie de Melun and a triple cream named after the 7th century bishop Saint Faron.
new.tip: Tours are by appointment only, Tuesday to Saturday. Production is best seen on weekday mornings.
new.q: Fromagerie de Meaux Saint-Faron, Rue Jehan de Brie, Meaux

new.title: Buy Moret barley sugar at the Maison du Sucre d'Orge
new.desc: Benedictine nuns at Moret invented this amber sweet in 1638, and it is still made with a 17th century method with no added colour or flavour. It comes as amber berlingots or clear sticks, and in tins such as the Renaissance box that copies a model shown in the neighbouring museum.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Saturday, with Sunday afternoons from May to September. The museum was closed for work, so check first.
new.q: Maison du Sucre d'Orge, Place Royale, Moret-sur-Loing

new.title: Try Nemours poppy sweets at Des Lis Chocolat
new.desc: This Nemours chocolatier took over the Moret barley sugar and also makes the Nemours poppy candy, a confection made in Seine-et-Marne for over a century. A newer site of 1,326 square metres combines production labs, a shop and a chocolate and poppy museum.
new.tip: The shop is at 6 rue Louis Blériot. Check the current opening times and museum visits.
new.q: Des Lis Chocolat, Rue Louis Blériot, Nemours

new.title: Dine at L'Ermitage Saint-Antoine in Barbizon
new.desc: Chef Cyrine Jarretie split the house into a gastronomic dining room and a more relaxed bistro, La Table de Lucienne. A small grocery run by the chef is open from 10 am to 9 pm, with tapas and scallops later in the day.
new.tip: Opening days vary, with service typically at lunch and dinner on Mondays, Thursdays to Sundays. Book ahead.
new.q: L'Ermitage Saint-Antoine, 51 Grande Rue, Barbizon

new.title: Share a communal table at La Folie Barbizon
new.desc: A hotel, restaurant and artist residence at 5 Grande Rue, where each room is linked to an artist. Chef Éric Fava cooks plant-based, organic, locavore dishes, served at a big communal table or as tapas at the bar, and the menu changes regularly.
new.tip: Book a dinner at the communal table. Visit the artistic rooms if you stay over.
new.q: La Folie Barbizon, 5 Grande Rue, Barbizon

new.title: Book a tasting menu at Papylles in Bois-le-Roi
new.desc: A gourmet restaurant run by young chef Thomas Briandet, who trained at the Shangri-La Paris. The name uses a y as a tribute to his grandfather. It sits between Fontainebleau and Barbizon, at the edge of the forest.
new.tip: A weekday lunch menu is the best value, with longer tasting menus in the evening. Book ahead.
new.q: Papylles, 7 rue Demeufve, Bois-le-Roi

new.title: Lunch at the Café de la Paix in Bourron-Marlotte
new.desc: Since 2018 chef Felipe Pires and his team have served accessible bistronomic cooking built on local produce in a historic 19th century building. Gault&Millau notes a fixed lunch menu at around 30 euros and a changing à la carte.
new.tip: Go for the lunch menu and then walk the painters' village. Check opening days first.
new.q: Café de la Paix, 59 rue du Général de Gaulle, Bourron-Marlotte

new.title: Have a drink on the Moulin de Nemours terrace
new.desc: A summer guinguette on the banks of the Loing with a food market and a view of the medieval château. You can take the helm of an electric boat from 6 pm for a floating aperitif. It is casual and good for families, with a pétanque court.
new.tip: Open daily in the warm season, to 11 pm or midnight at weekends. Go for sunset.
new.q: La Terrasse du Moulin de Nemours, Cour du Château, Nemours

new.title: Eat a seasonal bistro lunch at L'Orizon in Coulommiers
new.desc: A bistro in the centre of Coulommiers serving French brasserie cooking built on seasonal produce. It opened in February.
new.tip: Pair it with a visit to the Halle aux Fromages nearby. Book for weekends.
new.q: L'Orizon, 1 rue de la Pêcherie, Coulommiers

new.title: Order homemade bistro dishes at Le Trottoir
new.desc: A small Parisian-style bistro on the corner of Rue des Pelletiers and Rue Saint-Nicolas in the centre of La Ferté-sous-Jouarre. It serves homemade gourmet dishes, with starters around 4 to 8 euros and mains around 13 to 19.
new.tip: Opening hours differ by source, so call ahead.
new.q: Le Trottoir, 20 rue des Pelletiers, La Ferté-sous-Jouarre

new.title: Dine over the water at Le Moulin in Montévrain
new.desc: A bistronomic restaurant in a mill whose room spans an arm of the Marne, with a wooden terrace over the water. It serves creative seasonal dishes, all made in house, not far from Disneyland Paris.
new.tip: Ask for a table by the water. Check opening days and book ahead.
new.q: Le Moulin, 1 chemin de Quincangrogne, Montévrain

new.title: Dine in an enchanted forest at Wonderwoods
new.desc: Ephemera's first restaurant outside Paris is set in a full scale forest with fairy creatures, designed by the film set studio Henriette & Compagnie. It sits in the Imagi Park leisure space at Val d'Europe, and its cocktails are a highlight, with vegetarian dishes available.
new.tip: Book ahead and check current hours. Take the RER A to Val d'Europe.
new.q: Wonderwoods, 1 rue de l'Hymne à la Joie, Serris

new.title: Buy goat cheese at the Fromages de Chèvre Moret farm
new.desc: A goat farm at Tancrou with a farm shop selling crottins, logs and tomettes. At the Île-de-France farm goat cheese contest in Melun it won gold for its ash covered log and pyramid and for its small chèvre, and silver for its aged crottin.
new.tip: Call ahead to check shop hours. Buy a crottin and a log for a picnic.
new.q: Fromages de Chèvre Moret, Tancrou

new.title: Taste craft beer at the Second Degré microbrewery
new.desc: A microbrewery at 10 rue de l'Église in Magny-le-Hongre, brewing its own beer since 2020 and serving IPAs, porters and fruity sours with cheese boards. It seats up to 60 people and has a terrace.
new.tip: Reserve in advance, since the place is popular. Hours vary, so check before you go.
new.q: Microbrasserie Second Degré, 10 rue de l'Église, Magny-le-Hongre

new.title: Pick your own fruit at the Cueillette de Nolongues
new.desc: A pick-your-own farm in Jouarre run by Christophe and Claire-Marie Charpentier, listed by the Seine-et-Marne tourism board. It lets you gather fresh local produce straight from the field.
new.tip: Check what is in season and the opening dates before you go. Bring baskets.
new.q: Cueillette de Nolongues, Route de Nolongue, Jouarre

new.title: Buy farm cider at the Ferme de l'Abondance
new.desc: Charlotte and Arnaud Gronfier raise lamb and Aubrac cows and keep a cider tradition alive with organic petit jaune, judor and judeline apples. They make a brut and a demi-sec cider, plus organic apple juice, sold at the farm.
new.tip: No opening hours are posted, so call ahead. The farm is at Vaux-sur-Lunain.
new.q: Ferme de l'Abondance, 18 rue de Lorrez-le-Bocage, Vaux-sur-Lunain

new.title: Taste farm ice cream at Les 3 Givrées
new.desc: Three farming couples near May-en-Multien make ice cream and sorbet on site from the milk of their own cows, with about forty flavours. Fruit comes from nearby Seine-et-Marne growers, and the products carry the Produit en Île-de-France label.
new.tip: The farm shop opens Wednesday afternoon, Friday late afternoon and Saturday morning, all year.
new.q: Les 3 Givrées, 30 rue du Pré Gault, May-en-Multien

new.title: Sample local craft beer from the Brasserie des Grottes
new.desc: A Seine-et-Marne craft brewery near Melun making original local beers with quality ingredients and traditional techniques, listed by the Melun Val de Seine tourist board.
new.tip: Check whether the brewery shop is open before you drive out. The tourist office in Melun can help.
new.q: Brasserie des Grottes, Boissise-la-Bertrand
